data.title: Stocks: Correction, Bear Market, Or Something Much Worse?
data.description:
After several weeks of selling pressure, growing volatility, and significant declines in technology and AI-related stocks, investors are facing an important question: Is this a normal correction, the beginning of a cyclical bear market, or something much worse, similar to what unfolded after the major stock market peaks in 2000 and 2007?

Recent developments involving NVIDIA (NVDA) have added to uncertainty surrounding the AI trade. Despite reporting strong earnings and providing upbeat guidance, NVIDIA shares struggled as investors weighed leadership changes, regulatory scrutiny, and questions about the sustainability of massive AI-related investments.

Meanwhile, inflation remains a concern. Recent Federal Reserve communications suggest additional interest rate hikes may be necessary, raising questions about the potential impact of tighter monetary policy on economic growth, corporate earnings, and stock market valuations.

This week's video examines the weight of the evidence across multiple timeframes, including:

The S&P 500's recent correction and important technical support levels.

Historical drawdowns during the secular bull markets of 1950–1968 and 1982–2000.

Key distinctions between normal corrections, cyclical bear markets, and major secular trend changes.

Comparisons with the stock market peaks in 2000 and 2007.

The latest developments in the Nasdaq, semiconductors, and large-cap growth stocks.

Volatility, oversold conditions, market sentiment, and the potential for a sustained rebound.

Corporate earnings expectations and the longer-term outlook for stocks.

The importance of aligning investment decisions with our objectives and time horizon.

While recent market action has been unsettling, history reminds us that meaningful corrections can occur within powerful secular bull markets. At the same time, protecting capital during periods of prolonged secular stagnation remains an important consideration.

Is the long-term bullish case still intact, or is the market beginning to provide evidence of a more significant change?

We'll examine the charts, historical precedents, and current market evidence to better understand the probabilities and the guideposts that could help us navigate the weeks and months ahead.

data.title: Consequences For Excesses?
data.description:
Starting out with a quick follow-up from yesterday, as markets went down a lot again on Friday. Oddly though, the things I follow, more of them were up today in the bigger decline versus yesterday's slightly smaller decline. 

For a long time here and in client letters, we've been talking about obvious excesses in the tech sector while being clear that there was no way to know when or if there would ever be a consequence for those obvious excesses. If there was no way to know when or if there would be consequences, then the only protection was to be underweight versus the index. Zero weight was not/is not practical, but being underweight was/is practical. 

For the last six months, the iShares Semiconductor ETF (SOXX) is down 40%, as you can see. Since the beginning of October, SOXX is down 35%. I have no idea what will happen, but that seems awfully fast. I'm not trying to predict anything, more like just read the room. Fast declines tend to snap back quickly, so maybe this one will too?

Where we've spent a lot of time trying to understand autocallable ETFs, this event has been a great chance to learn more about how they behave when markets get hit. Some of the declines have been massive. Those are just Friday's declines.

I was talking to a buddy today who said he's concerned about all the stuff going on with outages and the like. I'm not really concerned that there will be some sort of societal-level breakdown, but similar to COVID, there could certainly be some inconveniences. If you haven't already done so, it's a good idea to add two-factor authentication to all your accounts. There's no reason not to have extra batteries on hand, a little cash in the house, get a little ahead on food (I'm not saying doomsday levels) and for us a little bit of gasoline which is for our ATV and generator. I'd say it's always a good idea to have some level of preparedness for emergencies if you want to think of it that way, or a little less dramatically, preparedness for inconveniences.

The rest of the post from here was written a couple of days ago, but events got in the way. 

The new iShares Macro AlphaBeta Active ETF (GMIX) takes a page out of ReturnStacked's playbook, allocating 100% to large-cap domestic equities and 100% to global macro, so it is leveraged. Here's a write-up from BlackRock in support of the new fund. 

iShares has a newer ETF that is in the macro realm with IALT, and so far, that fund has done pretty well. I saw some chatter, though, that the macro sleeve of GMIX might look more like PBAIX, which is a BlackRock fund I'd never heard of before. PBAIX is a 5-star fund, and it has done well, but I wouldn't say it's done better than some of the other macro funds we've looked at. As I learn more about it, maybe it will turn out that it takes a different path to a similar result as the others, which would make it interesting. 

RDMIX is a ReturnStacked product that, similar to GMIX, has 100% equity/100% macro. The latest incarnation goes back to the start of 2025. The ReturnStacked guys don't suggest 100% or 50% of a portfolio into their funds but the backtest maybe gives a little color on how equities and macro could work together. 

Staying in the macro realm, the other day we mentioned the Victory Pioneer Multi-Asset Income Fund (PMFYX). Despite the name, it is not a straightforward fixed income fund. It is legit multi-asset. Morningstar categorized it as Global Moderate Allocation. This is from the fund's July 30 factsheet.

It goes pretty far afield. A good portion of its high sixes yield comes from equity-linked notes in a similar manner as how JEPI uses equity-linked notes. That is not a precise explanation, but thinking of them as short-term autocallables might give some context. 

This chart is helpful for framing what I think are different objectives. PMFYX isn't really a stand-alone fixed income fund, and it doesn't trade that way. Similar to AQRIX it seems like a potential replacement for VBAIX, so maybe calling it macro isn't fair. PBAIX does look like a replacement for a stand-alone fixed income fund, at least what I think people want bond funds to look like with very low volatility and very shallow drawdowns. It hasn't had a down year in our ten-year backtest.

If you think you want to dabble in macro funds, I would suggest trying to draw a conclusion about what you think it is trying to do. Right or wrong, I don't think PBAIX is a replacement for VBAIX. Right or wrong, PMFYX very well could be...more so than PBAIX anyway.

You can decide for yourself whether the above is compelling or not. There's not much differentiation over time except in 2022. Portfolio 1 was down 6.01% that year; Portfolio 2 was down 8.45% compared to a drop of 16.87% for VBAIX. In other words, it differentiated when investors most needed it to. In 2023, 2024, and 2025, both were very similar to VBAIX, but this year, as bonds have struggled price-wise again, Portfolios 1 and 2 are way ahead again. 

This next chart throws a different type of macro fund into the mix with DYMIX.

It's a shorter lookback because DYMIX is a newer fund. DYMIX looks much different in terms of growth rate, volatility, and drawdowns. Higher growth rates aren't the only determining factor. Anyone who cares about this sort of alternative needs to consider not just the growth rate but how it would fit in with their other holdings. There's no way to know how well they will do in the future for their respective growth rates, but it is reasonable to conclude that PBAIX will be far less volatile than DYMIX.

In terms of correlations, I'd be more confident in PBAIX maintaining its low correlation to VBAIX, but based on DYMIX's volatility, I would expect the correlation to VBAIX to be more volatile too.

data.title: Dow, S&P 500 Join Nasdaq In Correction Territory
data.description:
Stocks were pummeled to end the week, with Wall Street getting rug-pulled by the reeling AI trade. The Dow shed 949 points for a fifth-straight loss, while the S&P 500 clocked its seventh-straight decline, its worst losing streak since February 2020. Both indexes are now officially in correction territory.

Not to be outdone, the Nasdaq dropped 1,261 points and is now in the red for 2026. All three major indexes finished with their worst weeks since April 2025. As investors adjust to this new reality, Wall Street's "fear gauge," the Cboe Volatility Index (VIX), traded at its highest level since March and logged its best week since April 2025. 

Steep Weekly Losses For Oil, Gold

Oil prices rose today but logged a third-straight weekly decline. Facing a supply surplus, December-dated West Texas Intermediate (WTI) gained 1.1% to settle at $84.09. The front-month January contract finished up 0.7% at $83.04. For the week, black gold is shed 5%. 

Gold prices turned in their worst week since March. December-dated futures shed 4.5% for the session to settle at $3,513.54 per ⁠ounce, while giving back 9.5% for the week.

data.title: CEE & CCA Week Ahead: Polish Activity Data And Czech Confidence In Focus
data.description:
Poland will release industrial output, labour market and retail sales data, while Czech confidence indicators are expected to show weaker consumer sentiment but a modest improvement in business confidence

Poland: Industrial weakness persists as consumption loses momentum

October industrial output and labour market data will be released on Monday. Fewer working days than in October 2025 mean that we should expect low-single-digit annual growth in industrial output, as the underlying trend remains lacklustre and uneven. Cost pressures in industry are mounting, pushing producer prices (PPI) higher. Recent readings suggest that price pressures not only stem from rising refining prices but are becoming increasingly broad-based. Nevertheless, this has not translated into stronger pressure on core consumer prices, as weak demand is forcing businesses to compress margins.

The labour market has stabilised, with wage growth in the enterprise sector slowing to below 6% year-on-year and employment continuing to decline. With demand for labour somewhat weaker, supply-side deterioration, reflecting the shrinking working-age population, is playing an increasingly dominant role. The unemployment rate remains low and among the lowest in the European Union.

October retail sales data follow on Tuesday. Fewer trading days and a high reference base for food sales will outweigh some recovery in fuel sales following another cut in VAT and excise duty on gasoline. We also see limited room for stronger sales of durable goods, which have proved surprisingly resilient to the strain on household finances from higher fuel bills and slowing wage growth. Consumption is projected to weaken further in the coming quarters as elevated uncertainty keeps the propensity to save high.

Czech Republic: Consumer confidence likely weakened on higher food prices

Consumer confidence likely deteriorated in November, with Tuesday's release expected to reflect the impact of rising food prices. That said, the consumer mood likely remained solidly above its long-term average, as households continue to benefit from decent nominal and real wage dynamics. In contrast, business confidence likely edged up in the same month, somewhat correcting its previous pronounced losses while remaining below its long-term average, pressured by rising input costs and ongoing uncertainty.

data.title: Q3 2026 U.S. Retail Scorecard - Update
data.description:
To date, 149 of the 183 companies in our LSEG Retail/Restaurant Index have reported their EPS results for Q3 2026, representing 81% of the index. Of those companies that have reported their quarterly results, 69% announced profits that beat analysts’ expectations, while 3% delivered on-target results and 28% reported earnings that fell below estimates. The Q3 2026 blended earnings growth estimate now stands at 8.7%.

The blended revenue growth estimate for the 146 companies in this index is 6.4% for Q3 2026. Of those companies that have reported their quarterly results so far, 59% announced revenue that exceeded analysts’ expectations and the remaining 41% reported that their revenue fell below analysts’ forecasts.

Exhibit 1: LSEG Earnings Dashboard

This week in retail

Walmart (WMT) delivered another robust quarter, exceeding earnings, revenue, and same store sales (SSS) expectations. Earnings increased 4.8% from a year ago, while revenue rose 5.2%. U.S. comparable sales increased 2.9%, although the result was affected by federal Medicare drug-pricing rules. Excluding that impact, comparable sales would have risen approximately 3.6%, suggesting underlying consumer demand was stronger than the headline figure indicates.

Sales growth was broad-based across categories, supported by continued market-share gains and a 23% surge in U.S. e-commerce, driven by strong pickup and delivery demand. Meanwhile, Walmart Connect — its U.S. advertising business — grew 37%, while global membership fee revenue increased 17%. Together, these higher-margin businesses provide Walmart with additional financial flexibility to invest in lower prices, strengthen customer loyalty and expand its competitive advantage.

The results reinforce a key theme this earnings season: consumers are still spending, but they are shopping more strategically. Both customer traffic and average ticket increased, while Walmart continued to gain market share across income groups, including households earning more than $100,000 annually. This suggests that value-seeking behavior is extending beyond lower-income shoppers, as even higher-income consumers become increasingly selective about where they spend.

E-commerce remains a particularly powerful growth engine. Walmart’s 23% digital growth reinforces a broader trend across retail, with Target (TGT), Home Depot (HD), and Lowe’s (LOW) also reporting strong online sales. The results suggest that convenience, faster fulfillment, and competitive pricing are increasingly influencing consumer purchasing decisions, making digital capabilities a critical differentiator in today’s retail environment.

Meanwhile, Williams-Sonoma (WSM) matched Q3 earnings expectations, with earnings increasing 11.6% from a year ago and revenue rising 5.8%. Comparable sales grew a healthy 5.1%, supported by positive performance across its brands and channels. The results highlight continued resilience among some higher-income consumers who remain willing to spend on premium home furnishings despite broader economic uncertainty.

Management emphasized the strength of its differentiated merchandise and operating model, noting that its design capabilities and direct sourcing strategy have supported increased full-price selling while maintaining a compelling value proposition. This combination of product differentiation, pricing discipline and operational efficiency helped support profitability during the quarter.

Williams-Sonoma also benefited from tariff-related income, which helped offset higher costs of goods sold, as well as increased interest income. Encouraged by its performance, the home furnishings retailer reiterated its fiscal 2026 outlook, signaling confidence in its ability to sustain momentum through the holiday season.

StarMine Signals Potential Earnings Surprises at Five Below (FIVE) and Ross Stores (ROST)

Looking ahead, value remains a dominant theme this earnings season, with consumers increasingly prioritizing affordability, compelling merchandise, and a differentiated shopping experience. Against this backdrop, LSEG StarMine models identify Five Below and Ross Stores as potential earnings outperformers heading into their upcoming Q3 announcements.

Sentiment is particularly favorable for Five Below, with consensus estimates calling for Q3 2026 EPS of $1.17 and SSS growth of 10.8%. More importantly, the StarMine Predicted Surprise exceeds 2%, signaling an elevated likelihood that the value retailer could outperform consensus earnings expectations and deliver a positive surprise (Exhibit 2).

Similarly, StarMine signals suggest that Ross Stores is well positioned to exceed earnings expectations, supported by continued demand for discounted branded merchandise. With consumers increasingly focused on stretching their purchasing power, the upcoming results from both retailers will provide further insight into the strength of discretionary spending and the competitive positioning of value-oriented retailers.

data.title: Palo Alto Networks Stock Soars On Strong FCF Guidance - Any More Upside Left In PANW?
data.description:
Palo Alto Networks (PANW), a cybersecurity software subscription company, reported strong free cash flow (FCF) margins and guided to 38% this fiscal year. PANW stock rose 8% on this guidance on Thursday after rising ahead of the results. Could it be worth more?

PANW is at $364.77, up more than 7.0% midday on Thursday, Nov. 19, after rising 9.9% on Wednesday from a recent low of $309.29 on Nov. 17 ahead of the Nov. 18 fiscal Q1 2027 earnings release (ending Oct. 31) after the market closed.

PANW stock - last 3 months - Barchart - Nov. 19, 2026

Moreover, analysts seem to be very positive on the stock. For example, Yahoo! Finance reports that the average price target (PT) of 54 analysts is $405.78, and Barchart's mean survey PT is $398.62. These PTs are only about 8% higher than Thursday's price (11/19).

So, is there much upside left in PANW?

FCF performance and high FCF Margin Guidance

Palo Alto Networks' fiscal Q1 revenue was up 39.25% YoY, and over the past year it rose 30.29%, according to Stock Analysis data.

Moreover, its adjusted free cash flow (FCF rose 13.1% to $1.937 billion YoY. However, its adj. FCF margin fell from 69.2% in Q1 last year to 59.6% in fiscal Q1 2027.

Nevertheless, on a trailing 12-month (TTM) basis (which is important since many of its clients renew subscriptions annually), the adj. FCF rose almost $1 billion from last year.

This can be seen on page 31 of its presentation deck. It shows that TTM adj. FCF rose from $3.75 billion last year to $4.638 billion in Q1 (+23.5%). It was even 5% higher than the Q4 TTM figure.

Palo Alto Networks - Adj. FCF trailing 12 months (TTM) - Q1 deck page 31 - Nov. 18, 2026

Note, however, that the TTM adj. FCF margin dipped slightly to 37.3% from 39.3% of revenue last year and even 38.4% in fiscal Q4.

However, management provided a 38.0% adj. FCF guidance for the year ending July 31, 2027. Let's see how that might work out. 

Forecasting FCF and Price Targets

Management expects its revenue to be between $14.52 billion and $14.57 billion. That's even higher than prior analysts' average forecasts of $14.4 billion.

For the next year, these analysts forecast $16.47 billion in revenue. So, over the next 12 months (NTM), revenue could be about $15 billion:

  $14.55b x 0.75 + $16.47b x 0.25 = $10.91b +$4.12b = $15.02 billion NTM revenue

So, applying a 38% margin, adj. FCF could hit $5.708 billion

That's over $1 billion higher than the $4.638 billion TTM figure shown above. In other words, its forecasted NTM adj. FCF could rise over 23%.

That certainly shows why the stock is up so much. But, how much is left?

For example, Palo Alto Networks' adj. FCF yield has averaged about 2.0% over the last year (i.e., a 50x multiple). So, applying this metric to its NTM adj. FCF forecast:

  $5.708 / 0.02 = $285.4 billion fair value

That's only about 2.5% above its present market cap of $278.32 billion today. And that implies a PT of $372.30. That's lower than other analysts' targets, as I showed above.

Even with a slightly better 1.85% FCF yield (i.e., a 54x multiple), the stock is worth just $308.54 billion, or +10.9% higher. That gives it a NTM price target of $402.81.

Summary and Conclusion

Palo Alto Networks produced strong adj. FCF with lower quarterly margins, including slightly lower TTM adj. FCF as a percent of revenue (37.3%). As a result, with management's guidance of 38% margin this year and applying this to a next 12-month (NTM) revenue forecast, its adj. FCF could hit $5.7 billion.

With a generous 54x multiple, that only implies a 10.9% higher price target for Palo Alto Networks. Nevertheless, the stock could exceed this at any time. 

But value investors have to take this into account when deciding whether its recent rise leaves any upside.

data.title: Why We Can’t Soak The Rich
data.description:
Source

Today we continue my series on debt and taxes. In brief, the federal government has a huge amount of spending, a less huge amount of tax revenue, and thus a huge debt. Almost everyone agrees we need to close this gap. We differ on how to do so.

Last week we looked at just income taxes. This week we are going to look at other types of US taxes as necessary groundwork for when we look at what the outcome of raising various taxes will be, either with or without accompanying spending cuts. Then we will start on how effective simply raising taxes will be. I expect that to be at least one if not two more letters.

There are two knobs we can turn: more/less spending and more/less taxes. We can turn one of them, both of them or neither of them. Specifically, can we make a dent in the debt by raising taxes on the wealthiest taxpayers? That’s politically appealing to some because it leaves most voters unaffected, though it may affect the economy by reducing growth as it has elsewhere. That being said, there is serious research that shows taxes can raised somewhat without too much drag on the economy, but nowhere near enough to solve the problem.

The problem with simply taxing the rich more, as you’ll see, is that it won’t solve the problem, because it changes behavior and thus eventual taxes. The debt will still be there and the voters we are trying to shield will still get hurt.

A Quick Look at Social Security

I will go deeper on Social Security in a future letter. It deserves more than a short mention. But since payroll taxes are a giant part of all federal revenue – and Social Security benefits comprise a giant part of federal spending – I want to run through a few preliminary numbers now.

Social Security at a Glance

Sources: SSA (wage base); 2026 Social Security Trustees Report as summarized by CRS and others; Mauldin Economics, John Mauldin

Because of the wage cap, the payroll tax is a flat tax up to $184,500 and zero above it. That makes it regressive at the top, which is exactly why "raise the cap" is always on the list of fixes. We will run those numbers when we get there.

Up to 85% of benefits can be subject to income tax for retirees above certain income thresholds. The tax on the first half of benefits goes back into the Social Security trust funds, about $58 billion in 2025; the tax on the portion between 50% and 85% goes to Medicare's hospital insurance fund. The income thresholds have not been adjusted for inflation since 1993, so every year more retirees get caught. This has quietly been propping up the trust funds. (See, sometimes inflation helps! – note sarcasm) The new senior deduction in last year's tax bill further reduced Social Security revenue, though temporarily as the $6,000 tax break expires in 2028.

Overall, the system’s costs have exceeded its tax revenue since 2010 and exceeded total income, including interest, since 2021. The trust fund is not a vault. It is an IOU from the Treasury, and the Treasury has to borrow to redeem it. As I said, this will take a full letter, because they’re just 100 nuances. There are almost 60 million Americans receiving Social Security.

The total Social Security beneficiary population (all ages) is over 76 million people in October 2026, but the vast majority are older adults. Most paid Social Security taxes for their entire adult lives and have the entirely reasonable expectation that they will get those benefits when they retire.

According to the U.S. Census Bureau’s analysis of survey responses matched with IRS tax and Social Security Administration benefit records, about 14%, or 22 million, older Americans receive 90% or more of their household income from Social Security. Survey data, which is subject to the vagaries of survey questions, suggest that the number might be as much as twice that. There are reasons for this discrepancy, and we will walk into that minefield in a later letter.

Corporate Tax Rates

The corporate income tax is a much smaller part of the picture than its political profile suggests, amounting to only about 7% of federal revenue last year. The 2017 tax law cut the rate from 35% to 21%. Here is what happened to receipts.

Corporate income tax receipts and the statutory rate.

Receipts fell sharply in the first three years after the cut, as everyone expected. Then they climbed to records: $425 billion in fiscal 2022 and $530 billion in fiscal 2024, far more than the government ever collected at 35%. Supporters of lower rates point to this as evidence that a lower rate can bring in as much or more revenue over time, by keeping profits and headquarters in the US and reducing the incentive to shift income abroad.

There is research behind that view. Kevin Hassett and Alex Brill found a corporate "Laffer curve" across developed countries, with the revenue-maximizing rate drifting down toward about 26%; Kimberly Clausing's basic estimate was about 33%. Both were above the 21% we have now, and both were below the 35% we had before 2017.

On the other hand, the Congressional Research Service disputes those findings and argues that most of the post-2021 surge reflects inflation and unusually high corporate profits rather than the rate cut. And receipts fell to $381 billion in fiscal 2026, in part because last year's tax law restored full expensing for business investment. This requires a little deeper dive.

First, the law that allows businesses to deduct ordinary and necessary business expenses was first established in the Internal Revenue Code of 1954, and has been amended several times since then, most recently and significantly in 2017 in the first Trump administration. Going forward, the details matter if we are going to consider raising corporate tax rates again.

  • Prior to 2025, 100% bonus depreciation had been available under the 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (TCJA) for qualified property placed in service between September 27, 2017, and the end of 2022

  • The TCJA introduced a phase‑out: 80% in 2023, 60% in 2024, 40% in 2025, 20% in 2026, and 0% by 2027

  • The OBBBA restored the 100% rate and made it permanent for qualified property placed in service after January 19, 2025 

  • This applies to most tangible personal property with a recovery period of 20 years or less, certain software, and other qualifying assets, allowing corporations to deduct the full cost in the first year instead of depreciating over time.

The purpose behind accelerated depreciation is to give businesses incentive to invest money sooner than they might otherwise. And it clearly works. And while it costs “tax revenue" to allow for earlier depreciation, over time it evens out. Let's say that a particular widget would normally depreciate over five years. It would be the same total deduction whether it is over one or five years, so over time, the revenues will equal out. But the theory is the economy is growing faster. The counterargument is that businesses will make the investment anyway. In some cases, this is very likely true. But not in all cases.

My own reading is that above some point higher corporate tax rates cost more in lost investment than they bring in, and that the 35% we had before 2017 was well above that point, one of the highest in the developed world. 21% is a great number as it makes us competitive with countries like Ireland that have lower rates. But could we increase it to 25% or some higher number? When we are raising taxes everywhere else because of the deficit and debt? If we are going to solve the debt crisis, everything has to be on the table.

Longtime readers will know that my default position is for lower taxes and smaller government. But in what I believe is the coming sovereign debt crisis, people of good faith on all sides are going to have to make compromises. And as I keep repeating, no one will like them. They will all be bad choices.

Here’s another look at a chart I shared last week. Note how the individual income tax and payroll taxes dwarf corporate income tax revenue.

Below the corporate tax are some even smaller categories: Tariffs, excise taxes (gasoline, etc.), estate and gift taxes, etc. These generate much more heat than they do money for the government. Even Trump’s new tariffs – which have caused real economic damage – are a rounding error in the big picture. They grew a lot in percentage terms, from $79.1 billion in FY 2024 to $194.9 billion in FY 2025. My preference would be to have a low and standard flat tariff if we have any tariff at all, rather than using tariffs as a hammer to bludgeon our trading partners. Are there cases can be made for a tariff? Yes, and they should be on the table.

Then there’s the estate tax. Very few estates actually pay it because very few estates are bigger than the excluded amount. The few that are bigger can usually avoid it by employing (perfectly legal) estate planning techniques. The estate tax is as close as we get to a “voluntary” tax. Anyone who actually pays it does so by default.

Now, About Taxing the Rich

We now have enough data to begin do the arithmetic. Let's first be generous to the idea and assume, unrealistically, that nobody changes their behavior. No one moves, no one realizes fewer capital gains, no one restructures a business or hires a better accountant. These are static numbers, using 2023 income against the 2026 deficit.

"Tax the Rich" vs. the Deficit (static estimates, no behavioral response)

Sources: IRS Statistics of Income via Tax Foundation (tax year 2023); CBO; Forbes; Mauldin Economics static calculations; Mauldin Economics, John Mauldin.

Read that table slowly. First note that the reason the top 1% only pay 26.3% of their income as taxes, is that much of their income is capital gains and other tax-favored income. They will pay the full 39.9% on their non-capital gain or tax-sheltered income. To get them to pay 40% you would have to exclude capital gains taxes above a certain number. Again, that assumes no behavior changes which is not realistic.

Raising the average tax rate on the top 1% by more than half, from 26.3% to 40%, which would require top marginal rates far above today's 39.9% (including the Medicare tax), raises about $430 billion on paper. That closes about a fifth of the gap. To close the whole deficit through the income tax on the rich, you would have to take essentially every dollar the top 1% earns, after what they already pay, and they would have to keep earning it anyway.

Static revenue from taxing the rich vs. the deficit.

Wealth taxes don’t escape the arithmetic either. The Forbes 400 are worth a record $8 trillion this year. Seize all of it, every share of every company, and you could pay for about four years of deficits. Once. Then it would be gone, along with the companies those shares represent being run by people with every incentive to make them grow.

And those are the generous numbers. In the real world, behavior changes. Top incomes are dominated by capital gains, which people can choose when to realize. Top-end income is also volatile: in 2023 the income of the top 1% fell 9%, mostly because of lower realized capital gains. We have been in an extraordinarily powerful bull market which allows for extraordinarily high capital gains. A bear market will eviscerate those potential gains.

Raise the rate sharply and gains get realized less often, held until death, or moved into structures that are taxed later or not at all. The revenue estimates shrink. That is Adam Smith's fourth maxim in action.

Let me be clear about what I am and am not saying. I am not saying the rich cannot or should not pay more. There may be good arguments for some increases at the top, and we will look at them fairly. What I am saying is that "tax the rich" cannot, by itself, come anywhere close to closing a $2 trillion deficit, much less pay for new spending on top of it. The math simply doesn’t work. The people making that promise are either not doing the arithmetic or hoping you will not.

The Scorecard

Pulling the key numbers together in one place:

IRS figures are tax returns, tax year 2023. CBO figures are households, 2023, and include payroll, corporate and excise taxes. n/a: not published on that basis. Sources: IRS SOI; Tax Foundation; CBO; Mauldin Economics, John Mauldin.

The rich pay most of the income tax already. The middle pays mostly payroll taxes (which are quite real, especially in percentage of total income terms). The bottom 40-50% as a group is a net recipient of government subsidies as we demonstrated last week. And the income tax, whatever its top rate, has brought in roughly 7% to 10% of GDP for 75 years.

Next, we have to ask an uncomfortable question. Suppose we tried to get the deficit below nominal GDP growth using taxes alone. How much would we need to raise? From whom? Through what kind of tax? Since 86% of revenue comes from individual income and payroll taxes, any serious income tax-only plan has to reach deep into the middle class, or find another revenue source. For instance, the average OECD country gets 31% of their tax revenues from consumption taxes, either direct sales taxes or the much larger case of value-added taxes (VAT).

In future letters we will look at what various rate increases would actually raise, what the economic research says about the drag on growth, and why most of the developed world funds its welfare states with broad consumption taxes as well as payroll taxes and income taxes rather than by taxing the rich even harder than we already do. (Regular readers will remember I have floated a VAT before, and I want to revisit that idea honestly, warts and all.)

Then we will turn to the other side: what we actually spend money on, line by line, and who depends on each line. Every item in the budget has a constituency. It is one thing to say health care is a large share of federal spending; it is another to tell a specific group of people their benefits will be cut.

Mathematically, you can close the gap with tax increases, spending cuts, or a combination. Politically, you can’t do it with only one of those. That’s why we will likely not do anything substantial until a crisis forces our hand. Stay tuned…

data.title: Progress Isn’t Protection
data.description:
This week, Microsoft (MSFT)’s Outlook service went down. A software problem disrupted banking transactions at JPMorgan Chase (JPM) and other major banks. And apparently one router in Arkansas triggered an air traffic control communications failure that brought departures across the country to a halt.

Meanwhile, in China, a battery-powered aircraft designed to carry 19 passengers completed its first flight with a crew aboard.

Extraordinary progress. Surprisingly fragile systems.

Those aren’t contradictory descriptions of the world we live in. They’re increasingly descriptions of the same world.

Consider Equinor (EQNR), the Norwegian energy company. As of Thursday, it was still working to contain a cyberattack. Yet the company’s oil and gas production was running normally, with no indication that data had been stolen or altered.

That’s an important distinction. Resilience doesn’t always mean preventing something from going wrong. Sometimes it means keeping the essential things working while you deal with what went wrong.

The electric aircraft offers a different lesson. China’s CE-25A flew about 37.5 miles with two pilots and a flight-test engineer aboard. It’s an engineering milestone. Just last week, a noted energy analyst told me battery-powered airplanes would never work at scale. This flight doesn’t settle that argument. A successful test and a commercially viable airline service are very different things.

Source: Gulf News

Still, it is worth paying attention to. The fact that it happened in China gives me another reason to reflect on what I saw during my recent visit.

The world is gaining extraordinary capabilities. But as we are learning, adding capabilities and reducing vulnerabilities aren’t necessarily the same thing.

Efficiency Isn’t Resilience

For decades, the global economy rewarded efficiency. The push was to make things wherever they’re cheapest, keep inventories lean, and automate what you can. For the most part, that approach worked.

Spare capacity costs money was the thinking of the day. So do backup suppliers and alternative ways of getting things done. When everything works, those costs are easy to question. When something fails, you discover what they were buying you.

Efficiency and resilience aren’t opposites. A well-run business needs both. The problem comes when we squeeze out every inefficiency without asking whether some of it serves a purpose.

The same question applies to countries. And, as I’ll get to in a moment, to you and me.

Still Connected. More Cautious.

This week’s APEC summit in Shenzhen offers a useful reminder that competing with another country and doing business with it are not mutually exclusive.

Mainstream media focused on Xi Jinping, Donald Trump, and Vladimir Putin sitting at the same table, discussing limits to nuclear weapons.  Those talks were taking place alongside an economic gathering with a different emphasis. At APEC, Xi called for more open trade, closer regional integration, and cooperation in artificial intelligence. I wouldn’t confuse that with an end to strategic competition. Nor would I confuse strategic competition with an end to trade.

The more useful question is where countries are willing to depend on one another—and where they want alternatives.

That’s how I think about resilience. Not complete self-sufficiency, not walking away from every relationship that carries risk. Rather, understanding which dependencies could leave you exposed and deciding what to do about them.

Shenzhen is an unusually good place to think about that question. It was the final stop on my eight-day trip through mainland China’s top-tier cities a few weeks ago.

A recent Bloomberg report describes the city as a showcase for China’s technological ambitions: Huawei, BYD (BYDDF), DJI, robotics, and artificial intelligence. It also describes a less comfortable side of the story—pressure on business profits and workers who aren’t sharing equally in the prosperity.

One parcel delivery worker told Bloomberg his monthly income had fallen from roughly 15,000 yuan a few years ago to about 9,000 yuan. That’s a substantial decline in a city producing some of the world’s most advanced technology.

One worker’s experience isn’t a measure of an entire economy. Nor does it establish that technology caused his pay to fall. But put those two pictures side by side: remarkable industrial capabilities and a household getting by on less.

Technological leadership and household financial security are not the same thing. Which brings up a question: What happens when a country becomes more resilient, but the people living inside it don’t?

Governments and large companies can devote enormous resources to securing supplies, developing alternatives, and protecting essential operations.

Individuals don’t always have that luxury.

The ability to adapt to change looks very different depending on whether you have savings, flexibility, and rising income—or are working harder to cover the same bills. That raises bigger questions about wages, work, and who benefits from technological progress.

There is a narrower question we can do something about today: How much of our financial life depends on everything working exactly as it should?

One phone. One email account. One bank. One copy of an important document.

We can’t control the pace of technological change or the relationship between Washington and Beijing. But we can identify a few points of failure in our own lives, and give ourselves alternatives.

I’m not suggesting you build a bunker, but if the world’s biggest powers are focusing on resilience, what does the same exercise look like for you and me?  

Here’s where I would start.

Protect Your Access

First and foremost, use strong, unique passwords for your important accounts. A password manager makes that much more manageable.

Strong passwords are the starting point, not the whole strategy. Turn on the strongest authentication your provider offers. Where available, phishing-resistant options such as security keys provide stronger protection than relying on a password alone.

Then learn how account recovery works. I can tell you from firsthand experience: The time to figure out how to regain control of an important account is well before you lose access. Once you are locked out, you are operating from a position of weakness. Not fun.

Keep recovery codes somewhere secure that you can reach even if your phone is unavailable. Think through the obvious question: If my phone disappeared tomorrow, how would I get back in?

Protect your phone number, too. Ask your carrier how to block unauthorized SIM changes and transfers of your number to another carrier. These aren’t necessarily the same setting. Verizon (VZ) and AT&T (T) both offer SIM Protection and Number Lock features.

And give your wireless account the same attention you give your financial accounts.  Using a lame password to protect your wireless account is an invitation to a world of trouble.

Keep Your Own Records

Download your financial institutions’ monthly statements, including holdings and share counts—not just a screenshot of the balance.

Keep copies of your insurance policies and other important documents somewhere you can reach them if your usual account or device is unavailable.

The key is not to create another single point of failure.

A copy on the laptop next to you isn’t much help if both copies disappear with the laptop. And an external drive attached to your computer is not an offline backup.

Keep a secure backup somewhere other than your house. At least one backup should also be disconnected from your computer when it isn’t being updated. Occasionally check that you can actually restore the files. A backup and process that you’ve never tested is an assumption, not a plan.

Have an Alternative

Governments and large companies often maintain more than one supplier. Consider applying that same thinking to your financial life.

If your day-to-day banking runs through one institution, a second banking relationship may be worth considering. The point isn’t to predict which bank might have a problem. It’s to avoid having every option depend on the same system.

Have some cash on hand.  In our increasingly cashless society, a stash of $20s can get you out of a short-term jam, be it cyber, weather, or institutional in nature.

Review your insurance with the same mindset. Ask what is covered, what is excluded, and where you may be assuming protection you don’t actually have.  For example, do you have cyber coverage, and if not, should you? Don’t wait until it’s too late to find out.

Make a Family Plan

Precautions are less useful if only one person in the household knows how they work.

Make sure your spouse or another trusted person knows where to find essential information and what to do if you’re unavailable.

Have a safe word or phrase that you, your spouse, and your kids know but never share.  Don’t email it to each other.  Set the safe word in person.  This is a way to verify identity if you get an unexpected request for money. Its purpose is to give everyone permission to pause and verify, rather than act under pressure. Keep the plan simple enough that your family will remember it when they’re worried or distracted.

A Little Preparation Goes a Long Way

The goal here isn’t to anticipate every possible failure. It’s to make sure one failure doesn’t become five.

I’m enthusiastic about what technology can do. What I saw in China gave me plenty to think about. I expect the coming years to bring advances that improve our lives in ways we haven’t yet imagined. I also expect the advances to come at us more and more quickly, and that can cause problems.

data.title: Gold Extends Decline As Rate Hike Expectations Weigh On Prices
data.description:
Gold (XAU/USD) continues to fall as expectations for further Fed tightening weigh on prices. The break below key weekly support adds to the risk of further declines. The upcoming PCE inflation report could shape interest rate expectations. Stronger inflation may increase pressure on gold, while softer data could support a recovery. Gold also needs to regain its former support area to improve its technical outlook.

Gold under Pressure Ahead of Key PCE Inflation Report

Gold continues to move lower as expectations for further Fed tightening offset the benefit of falling oil prices. WTI crude has lost more than 20% in November, while gold has declined about 8%. Lower energy costs have therefore provided little relief. Tariffs and rising technology costs may keep underlying inflation elevated even as cheaper oil reduces energy expenses. Persistent inflation keeps the focus on interest rates. Higher rates increase the opportunity cost of owning gold because it pays no interest. A stronger dollar also raises its cost in other currencies.

October meeting minutes showed that some Fed officials would consider a larger December increase if inflation data deteriorated. Christopher Waller also raised the possibility of a half percentage point increase or faster subsequent tightening. These messages support the dollar and limit gold recoveries.

The BEA will release October PCE inflation data on November 25. A monthly core reading above the expected 0.3% could support expectations for December and January rate increases. A reading of 0.1% or less could reduce those expectations and support gold. Preliminary November business surveys will also influence the dollar. If Fed officials push back against faster rate increases, gold could find additional support.

Gold Breaks below Weekly Descending Triangle Support

The gold chart below shows a descending triangle with a falling upper boundary and a horizontal base around $3,850 to $4,000. Gold failed to remain above this support area and continued to move lower. The red circle marks the final recovery attempt near the triangle floor. The large weekly decline extends below the former support range. This breakdown shifts attention toward lower historical support levels.

The $3,500 area provides the first nearby reference. Below it, the dashed horizontal support lies near $3,450. This line marks a previous price ceiling before the earlier advance accelerated. A test could slow the decline, but gold needs to establish a base to signal stability. A sustained move below $3,450 would expose the former consolidation area around $3,200 to $3,400. A stable base around these levels could support a recovery, while further declines would keep the outlook negative.

Any recovery initially faces resistance around $3,850 to $4,000. Gold must regain this former support area and remain above it to weaken the breakdown signal. The falling trendline marks the next resistance area as it slopes toward $4,200. A sustained move above that boundary would provide stronger evidence of a trend change. Until then, recoveries may remain vulnerable to renewed declines.

Gold Outlook: Downside Risks Persist Ahead of PCE Inflation

Gold retains a negative outlook as Fed tightening expectations and the weekly triangle breakdown point in the same direction. The immediate downside references are $3,500 and approximately $3,450. Stronger inflation could increase pressure on these levels. Softer data may support a recovery, but lasting technical improvement requires gold to reclaim $3,850 to $4,000. The response to PCE inflation will help determine whether the decline extends or begins to stabilize.

data.title: GM Backs $550 Million Solar Investment In Largest Clean Energy Deal To Date
data.description:
General Motors (GM) announced its largest clean energy investment to date, with the automotive giant signing a deal for 276 MW of energy, serving as the primary customer for two new solar facilities in Michigan developed by NorthStar Clean Energy.

According to GM, the new projects represent a combined investment of approximately $550 million, and are expected to generate roughly 539,000 megawatt-hours of electricity annually.

The new agreements follow an announcement earlier this year by GM that it had secured enough renewable energy to match 100% of electricity consumption across its U.S. facilities in 2025, becoming the first U.S. automaker to reach the milestone.

Under the new deal, GM will serve as the primary customer through a virtual power purchase agreement (VPPA) for the Branch Solar project in Branch County and Lake Iris Solar project in St. Clair County.

According to GM, the facilities are expected to generate electricity equivalent to the combined annual electricity consumption of three of the company’s Michigan assembly plants, Factory ZERO, Flint Assembly and Lansing Delta Township Assembly.

GM said that it plans to apply renewable energy credits generated by the projects toward emissions associated with electricity purchased for its manufacturing operations. The company added that it has reduced its Scope 1 and 2 greenhouse gas emissions by 52% since 2018.

Casandra Garber, Chief Sustainability Officer, GM, said:

“For GM, long-term renewable energy helps us manage costs, strengthen the operations behind the vehicles, batteries, and technologies we build, and advance our zero-emissions vision. It’s a practical example of how sustainable business and economic growth can reinforce each other.”

data.title: The Euro Takes A Priced-In Hike Into A Week That Belongs To American Inflation
data.description:
1.1000 has turned EUR/USD back in each of the past three sessions, and it did so in a week when most of the news leaned the Euro's way. Eurozone core inflation was revised higher, the ZEW sentiment survey beat its forecast, and the US factory numbers missed. The pair trades just above 1.0950 regardless, its lowest in 19 months, and has gone nowhere since Monday's break of the round number.

Good news for the Euro bought nothing above 1.1000

Eurostat's final October figures on Wednesday put core inflation at 2.6% YoY, up from a first estimate of 2.5%, and confirmed the headline rate at 4.0%. Tuesday's ZEW survey of economic sentiment came in at 26.5 against a 19.1 forecast. Traders put the odds of a European Central Bank (ECB) hike on December 17 above 90%, a move that would take the deposit rate from 2.50% to 2.75%.

The pair made its low for the year on the day of the inflation revision. A hike that's more than 90% priced has less than 10% left to add to a currency, so stronger inflation data now confirms a decision the market has already traded.

The Fed voted to hold and has argued about hiking ever since

The US calendar leaned the Euro's way as well. The Empire State and Philadelphia Fed factory surveys both came in at less than half their forecasts, industrial production fell 0.4% in October, and weekly jobless claims rose to 203K.

The Dollar didn't need the data. Minutes of the Fed's October meeting, released on Wednesday, showed almost all officials expect further hikes and a couple open to more than a quarter-point in December, and Fed Governor Waller asked for a half-point the same day. The Fed's rate is 3.75%-4.00% against the ECB's 2.50%, a gap of at least 1.25 points before either moves. October's vote was 10-2 to hold, both dissenters wanted a hike, and the committee has spent November debating how quickly to do what it voted not to do.

A December hike raises France's bill too

An ECB hike doesn't land evenly across the bloc. The extra yield investors demand to hold French 10-year debt over Germany's reached about 1.6 points earlier in November, the widest since the Eurozone debt crisis, and France's 2027 budget is still being fought over in parliament. Bank of France Governor Moulin said on Friday that France faces a budget crisis and is in a very different situation from Greece, the second time since early October he has raised the comparison in order to dismiss it.

For EUR/USD, higher ECB rates lift the yield on holding Euros and the cost of rolling French debt at the same time, which may be why a well-flagged hike hasn't put a floor under the pair. European Union (EU) leaders meet on November 26 and 27 with that budget fight unresolved.

PMIs, then PCE, then an account of a meeting already traded

The Hamburg Commercial Bank (HCOB) Purchasing Managers Index (PMI) surveys for November are due on Monday at 09:00 GMT, after a composite reading of 51.7 in October, with the US versions at 14:45 GMT. ECB Chief Economist Lane speaks the same day at 14:30 GMT.

Wednesday at 13:30 GMT is the release that matters most to the pair: October core Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) inflation, forecast at 3.2% YoY after 3.1%, alongside a first estimate of third-quarter Gross Domestic Product (GDP) forecast at 3.5% annualized. Traders pared their December Fed bets on Friday as US stocks sold off, so a core number at or above forecast could rebuild them and take the pair through 1.0950. A miss would hand the Euro a second look at 1.1000 with the Fed's preferred measure on its side.

US markets are shut on Thursday for Thanksgiving, which leaves the ECB's account of its October 29 meeting, due at 12:30 GMT, to a thin market. The account will show how close the Governing Council came to hiking in October, which is detail about a decision traders have already made on its behalf.

Technical levels

Resistance: 1.1000 has capped three straight sessions, with each high within about 10 pips of it. Above it, 1.1050 is where the pair paused on November 12 and 13 before breaking lower, and 1.1100 is the October floor it fell through on November 11.

Support: Wednesday's low just above 1.0950 is the 19-month low and has held on both sessions since. There's no 2026 level beneath it on the daily chart, which leaves 1.0900 as the next round number.

Bias: The lean is short while the pair stays under 1.1000. A daily close below 1.0950 targets 1.0900 first and 1.0850 after it. The daily Stochastic Relative Strength Index (Stoch RSI) is in the mid-40s and falling, so momentum isn't stretched enough to argue for a bounce on its own. A daily close above 1.1050 would put the pair back in the range it broke, and the short case ends there.

data.title: Preliminary Regional Fed Manufacturing Reports Suggest Inflation Is Spreading Downstream
data.description:
In discussing the ISM manufacturing index several weeks ago, I concluded that it “reminded me of the regional Fed reports for the last month, which suggested that while the expansion is intact, the second derivative may be declerating, i.e., the rate of growth has been peaking; and further that its inflationary component is accelerating, which is not good for downstream consumer prices.”

Here’s what the new orders component of that index looked like:

Well, now we have three regional Fed bank reports for November: New York, Philadelphia, and Kansas City, which give us our first look at how manufacturing is doing this month. The first two do get picked up by FRED, so let’s see what their averages can tell us.

First of all, the headline numbers (bue) declined -6.2 to 7.0, which suggests at least that the growth rate is stabilizing and possibly decelerating somewhat.  But, unlike the ISM report at the beginning of this month, the average of the new orders component (red) was the lowest since last year, as it decelerated sharply, by -12.4, to 1.3:

Meanwhile, the respective numbers from the Kansas City Fed constrasted significantly, as the headline regional index rose 7 to 18, and the new orders component rose 13 to 16.

Put all three together and the picture is of a stabilizing topline, and at very least the proverbial bloom might be coming off the rose somewhat as to new orders.

There might be an even more significant amplification present is in the prices component, and specifically prices received from downstream customers (red in the graph below). Prices paid declined -1.3 to 52.0, suggesting the torrid spread of price increases in that component has persisted. But even more signficantly, prices received rose 1.2 to 37.1. The last two months have been the highest readings in that entire series since the start of the Millennium outside of the post-pandemic period:

The regional Kansas City index suggested the same, with prices paid declining -17 to 53, and prices received rising 4 to 30.

In short, producers appear more determined, and able, to pass on higher prices to downstream customers, suggesting that consumer inflation, at least in the goods sector, is not going to slow in the next several months, and may even increase further. And keep in mind that real aggregate nonsupervisory payrolls may go negative YoY as early as next month if there is such a pass-through of inflation and a tepid employment report. In that regard, the best news in the surveys was that employment average rose 5.4 to 1.8:

All well and good for the present, but if corporate profits come under pressure, and real wages come under pressure as well, needless to say that would not be good.

November 17 – New York Times (Sabrina Tavernise, Georgia Gee and Madaleine Rubin): “In five short days, Americans have begun to wonder if their country is actually breaking. It started last Thursday, with the Microsoft outage. Then, on Friday, came the nationwide flight stoppage, only the third this century. History’s greatest Bubble was always going to end badly. It just went on for so long and to such outrageous extremes. Reckless monetary inflation; egregious speculation and leverage; epic malinvestment; deplorable wealth inequality and corruption. And we’ve reached the point where trust in government and our institutions is at such a low ebb. I can’t imagine a more precarious environment for managing financial, economic, social and geopolitical crises.

The unfolding crisis will present a major test for the “Fed put.” Speculative deleveraging will require another major inflation in the Federal Reserve balance sheet. They don’t expect to have to do it; they seemingly don’t have a plan to do it; but they will have no choice.

I come back to the same two questions: Will they move swiftly and in significant size to stabilize markets and restore confidence before things spiral out of control? Understandably, their current focus is to raise rates and get inflation under control. And they face the uncertainty of a highly unstable Treasury market – and how bonds might respond to another big round of QE, with the economy running hot, inflation elevated, and deficit spending completely out of control.

Fed President Hammack is certainly on the right track - though our central bank has run out of time. The Warsh Fed faces one hell of a challenge. It appears the whole world faces a hell of a challenge.

data.title: Is The Bottom In Sight For Gold? Let’s Check Some Unusual Stats

Even in the midst of this brutal precious metals smackdown, two things are virtually guaranteed:

A New Twist On Seasonality

Biggest Buyers Are Bargain Hunting

A gold/silver ratio (the number of silver ounces it takes to buy one gold ounce) above 90 usually signals rising precious metals prices. After falling way below that level earlier this year, the ratio is now spiking in the right direction.

Crisis = Opportunity

data.title: Lagarde Sees A €23 Billion Opportunity: Can Tokenization Finally Unite Europe’s 27 Markets?
data.description:
European Central Bank (ECB) President Christine Lagarde said on Friday, November 20, that tokenization could give Europe something it has chased for decades: one market for financial assets instead of 27. She warned that the chance may not last, because the market is growing fast and its rules are still being written.

She made the case in a keynote at the Frankfurt European Banking Congress. She told the room it was her eighth speech there as ECB President, and her last.

Tokenization means issuing assets such as bonds, shares or fund units as digital tokens on a blockchain, where they can be traded and settled in one place. Europe’s own digital money, though, is still tiny next to the dollar’s. We compared euro and dollar stablecoins to see how far behind it is.

Lagarde Calls Tokenization a Chance for a Single Market

Lagarde spent most of the speech on why Europe acts too late on slow-moving problems. Tokenization was one of three areas where she said the ECB had tried to act early. The other two were the digital euro and the euro’s role abroad.

“With the right framework, tokenisation offers a chance to build a genuine single market in digital assets, integrated from the start. For Europe, that is a huge opportunity,” she said in the speech published by the ECB.

The catch is timing. Lagarde said the global market for tokenized assets was worth around €23 billion in March, five times its size a year earlier. As it grows, its standards will set.

She warned that if standards develop separately, the market could split into platforms that follow different rules and cannot settle with one another. Europe’s stock and bond markets already work that way, with separate national systems that have proved very hard to merge.

Pontes and Appia Are the ECB’s Tokenization Tools

The ECB has already built part of the plumbing. In September, it launched Pontes, a link that lets tokenized trades settle in central bank money, the safest form of money there is, on Eurosystem systems. Every platform can now use the same settlement asset.

Earlier this month, the European Stability Mechanism, the euro area’s rescue fund, settled a €1 billion bond issued directly as a token on Pontes.

A second project, Appia, is working with banks and other firms on common standards for an integrated European market. But Lagarde said the central bank cannot finish the job alone. “Infrastructure alone is not enough. Common rules will be needed too, and those lie with legislators,” she said.

Euro Stablecoins Are Small Next to Dollar Tokens

Stablecoins are tokens pegged to a currency, and they are the cash leg of most crypto and tokenized trades today. On that front, Europe is far behind.

Dollar stablecoins in circulation total about $283.7 billion, while euro stablecoins total about $815 million. That is $1 in euro tokens for every $348 in dollar tokens, or a 0.29% share.

The euro side is growing faster from its small base. Since the stablecoin rules in the EU’s Markets in Crypto-Assets (MiCA) law took effect on June 30, 2024, euro stablecoins have grown 244%, while dollar stablecoins grew 76%. That doubled the euro’s share, from 0.15% to 0.29%.

One issuer dominates. Circle’s EURC accounts for about 62% of the euro total, ahead of SG-Forge’s EURCV.

This is why the ECB wants tokenized trades in Europe to settle in central bank money rather than in private tokens. In a market run on dollar stablecoins, European tokenization would depend on a currency the ECB does not control.

data.title: PayPal Stock Falls As Leadership Shake-Up Tests Turnaround Strategy
data.description:
PayPal stock PYPL fell 4% on Friday after the payments company announced a series of leadership changes as part of its turnaround efforts under CEO Enrique Lores.

The appointments include a new chief financial officer and executives overseeing consumer financial services, payments and artificial intelligence operations.

The company said the changes follow several months of strategic planning aimed at clarifying priorities across its core businesses, simplifying its operating model and strengthening leadership accountability.

However, the management overhaul comes as investors remain cautious about PayPal's ability to revive growth and regain market share.

PayPal has lost about 7% over the past 12 months.

The stock has also fallen approximately 82% from its all-time closing high of $308.53 reached on July 23, 2021.

PayPal appoints new CFO and business heads

Claire Bramley, currently CFO of cloud-based accounting software provider Xero, will join PayPal as executive vice president and CFO on February 1, 2027.

She will replace Jamie Miller, who has served as chief financial and operating officer.

Bramley will work with Miller during February to support the transition.

Bramley previously held senior finance positions at HP, where her tenure overlapped with Lores.

PayPal also appointed Kartik Mani as president and head of Consumer Financial Services and Venmo.

Mani joins from American Express, where he was president of Global Network and Partner Services. Venmo general manager Alexis Sowa will continue in her role and report to him.

Suzan Kereere, who currently leads PayPal's Global Markets business, will become president and head of Payment Services and Crypto.

She will succeed Jeff Pomeroy, who had been serving as interim head and will continue leading Payment Services and Platforms, reporting to Kereere.

Juan Rio will join the company on November 30 as executive vice president of AI Business Transformation and Operations.

He previously worked at Brightstar.AI as managing director and chief delivery officer. Rio will oversee AI initiatives, cost simplification and enterprise operating effectiveness.

Separately, PayPal announced that Chief Risk Officer Aaron Webster would leave the company.

Ratinder Bedi, senior vice president of Credit and Fraud Risk, will serve as interim head of the risk organisation while PayPal searches for a permanent replacement.

Board appointment and investor concerns

PayPal also appointed Brian J. Lee to its board of directors, effective November 30, 2026.

Lee served as Goldman Sachs' chief risk officer from 2019 to January 2025 and most recently chaired its Risk Council through October 2026.

The leadership changes come as Wall Street analysts remain divided over PayPal's prospects.

Of the 45 analysts covering the stock, 31 have a Hold rating, seven recommend selling, and seven have a Buy rating.

Monness Crespi Hardt analyst Gus Galá recently downgraded PayPal to Sell from Neutral and set a $48 price target.

He cited market-share losses and unfavourable business trends, including a year-over-year decline in third-quarter transaction revenue from PayPal's products and services.

Analysts at Freedom Broker, Cleveland Research and Bank of America have also recently downgraded the stock.

Analysts assess PayPal's growth engines

Not all analysts are negative on the company. Susquehanna analyst James Friedman maintains a Positive rating and a $67 price target.

Friedman believes PayPal's growth prospects should not depend entirely on its traditional branded checkout business.

He identified buy now, pay later services, Venmo, and Braintree's value-added merchant tools as three newer growth engines, each of which has recorded double-digit growth.

He argued that the traditional checkout business may only need to achieve modest growth of 2% to 3% to support overall profit expansion.

Friedman also expects PayPal to treat 2027 as an investment year, directing spending towards these three growth areas while using internal cost savings to keep overall earnings steady.

The turnaround, which Lores has led since joining in March, has focused on cost reductions and greater adoption of artificial intelligence.

PayPal's fourth-quarter results, expected in early February, will provide investors with an opportunity to assess management's progress.

Forward guidance and updates on the turnaround strategy are likely to remain central to the market's assessment of the company's new leadership team.

data.title: Circular Financing Doesn’t End With Nvidia: Amazon And Google Edition
data.description:
Jensen Huang’s sudden departure from Nvidia (NVDA) called attention to extent that the company was using its profits and credit standing to support the customers for its chips. Between direct equity stakes, loans, and loan guarantees, Nvidia was to a large extent funding the purchases of its chips. Its role in financing customers has been so large that its likely demand for its chips will fall off sharply with a Nvidia CEO less willing to engage in dubious financing arrangements.

But the Anthropic IPO is an opportunity to remind people that the circular financing in the AI industry goes beyond Nvidia. Both Amazon (AMZN) and Alphabet (GOOGL) are major holders of Anthropic stock. Amazon made an $8 billion equity investment in Anthropic in 2023 and 2024.  It bought another $5 billion this year. Alphabet put up 2022 and another $10 billion this year. Both companies have committed to buying more stock after the IPO.

This equity investment both directly and indirectly helped Anthropic pay for the computing power that Anthropic is buying from these companies’ data centers. The direct impact is straightforward. The indirect impact is that the money from these huge, well-established companies was a tremendously important vote of confidence that made other investors more willing to give their money to Anthropic. 

To be clear, there is nothing wrong with a major company investing in a promising startup that also happens to be a customer. But it is worth noting that a substantial portion of the money that Anthropic is using to buy computing power from Amazon and Alphabet is coming directly or indirectly from Amazon and Alphabet.

The other side of this story is also noteworthy. The value of the Anthropic shares held by these companies has risen enormously since they bought their stakes. This was booked as profit for these companies. In Amazon’s case, roughly half of its income for the first nine months of 2026 is the result of the appreciation of its Anthropic holdings. In Alphabet’s case, the impact of Anthropic’s appreciation was smaller, but together with its holdings of SpaceX, stock gains accounted for $77 billion, or roughly one-third of the company’s earnings over the last year.

These figures are important to keep in mind when considering reported price-to-earnings ratios. In Amazon’s case, while the reported price-to-earnings ratio is 21, measured against profits from operations it would be close to 40. In Alphabet’s case, the reported price-to-earnings ratio would be adjusted upward from roughly 15 to 20, if it is measured against operating profits. The stock prices of these companies look seriously more elevated when adjusted for these one-time stock gains.  

The moral of the story is that the financing of AI may prove to be more complicated than the technology.
